summary: This standards-track RFC describes using the ChaCha stream cipher and Poly1305 authenticator in TLS and DTLS, defining cipher suites that use them. It updates RFCs 5246 and 6347.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7905 adds a new option for encrypting TLS and DTLS connections. It uses two algorithms from the same author, ChaCha20 for encrypting and Poly1305 for detecting tampering. Both run quickly in ordinary software, without special hardware, which makes them useful on small devices. Seven new cipher suites are defined, and each one names a key exchange method and the new algorithms.

subtitle: Two fast, software-friendly primitives become a new family of cipher suites for TLS and DTLS.

tldr.problem: The CBC-mode cipher suites and the RC4 stream cipher in TLS and DTLS had known attack problems, and the existing AES-GCM suites raised concerns about performance and ease of software implementation.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines seven cipher suites built on the AEAD_CHACHA20_POLY1305 algorithm, with a 96-bit nonce formed from the record sequence number and the write IV, so no explicit per-record nonce is sent.
tldr.outcome: TLS 1.2 and DTLS 1.2 gain a stream-cipher option that is meant to be comparable to RC4 in speed and easy to implement without software side-channel weaknesses. RFC 7905 is itself updated by RFC 10015.

today: RFC 7905 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 5246 and RFC 6347. It is itself updated by RFC 10015, and no RFC obsoletes it.

sections.title: Why a New Cipher for TLS
sections.content:
This document describes the use of the ChaCha stream cipher and the Poly1305 authenticator in version 1.2 or later of the Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol, defined in RFC 5246, and in version 1.2 or later of the Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) protocol, defined in RFC 6347.

Recent attacks had shown problems with the CBC-mode cipher suites in TLS and DTLS, and with RC4, the only supported stream cipher. The existing authenticated encryption suites, which are based on AES-GCM, address some of these issues, but there are concerns about their performance and their ease of software implementation.

The RFC therefore sets out to describe a secure stream cipher for both TLS and DTLS that is comparable to RC4 in speed across a wide range of platforms, and that can be implemented easily without being vulnerable to software side-channel attacks. A side-channel attack here means one that learns information from how long an implementation takes or from what it caches, rather than from breaking the mathematics of the cipher.
sections.plainLanguage: Several cipher suites in TLS had known weaknesses, and the newer AES-GCM suites were hard to run quickly in plain software. This RFC adds a different option: a stream cipher with an authenticator that is fast in software and does not leak information through timing or cache behaviour.

sections.title: The ChaCha20 Stream Cipher
sections.content:
ChaCha is a stream cipher developed by D. J. Bernstein in 2008. It is a refinement of Salsa20, which was one of the selected ciphers in the eSTREAM portfolio, and ChaCha was used as the core of BLAKE, which was a finalist in the SHA-3 competition.

The variant used here has 20 rounds, a 96-bit nonce and a 256-bit key. It is called ChaCha20, and it is the conservative variant of the ChaCha family with respect to security. It is described in RFC 7539.
sections.plainLanguage: ChaCha20 encrypts a stream of bytes using a 256-bit key. It takes a 96-bit nonce, which is a value that must not repeat under the same key, and runs 20 rounds of mixing to produce the keystream. It is a refinement of Salsa20 and was the core of the BLAKE hash function.

sections.title: The Poly1305 Authenticator
sections.content:
Poly1305 is a Wegman-Carter one-time authenticator designed by D. J. Bernstein. It takes a 256-bit one-time key and a message, and produces a 16-byte tag that authenticates the message, so that an attacker has a negligible chance of producing a valid tag for a message that is not authentic. It is described in RFC 7539.

Both primitives were designed for high performance in software. They typically admit a compact implementation that uses few resources and inexpensive operations, which makes them suitable on a wide range of architectures. They were also designed to minimize the leakage of information through side channels.
sections.plainLanguage: Poly1305 checks that a message has not been changed. It takes a key that is used once, the message, and returns a 16-byte tag. The receiver recomputes the tag and compares it, so a modified message is rejected. The tag is short, and computing it needs only cheap operations.

sections.title: Building the Nonce for Each Record
sections.content:
The ChaCha20 and Poly1305 primitives are built into an authenticated encryption algorithm, AEAD_CHACHA20_POLY1305, as described in RFC 7539 and in the interface of RFC 5116. TLS and DTLS incorporate that algorithm as specified in Section 6.2.3.3 of RFC 5246.

The algorithm needs a 96-bit nonce, and the RFC defines how it is built. First, the 64-bit record sequence number is serialized as an 8-byte big-endian value and padded on the left with four 0x00 bytes. Second, that padded sequence number is XORed with client_write_IV when the client is sending, or with server_write_IV when the server is sending. In DTLS, the 64-bit sequence number is the 16-bit epoch concatenated with the 48-bit sequence number.

This construction differs from the one used with AES-GCM in TLS 1.2, but matches the scheme expected to be used in TLS 1.3. The nonce is built from the record sequence number and the shared secret, both of which the recipient already knows. The advantage is that no per-record explicit nonce has to be transmitted, which saves eight bytes per record and prevents implementations from mistakenly using a random nonce. In the terms of RFC 5246, SecurityParameters.fixed_iv_length is twelve bytes and SecurityParameters.record_iv_length is zero bytes.
sections.plainLanguage: Each record needs a nonce, and this RFC builds it from what the two ends already share. The record number is written as 8 bytes with four zero bytes in front, and that whole 12-byte value is XORed with the key material for the sending direction. Because both ends can work it out, nothing extra is sent with the record, which saves 8 bytes per record and removes the chance of a random nonce being used by mistake.

sections.title: The Cipher Suites and Their Code Points
sections.content:
The RFC defines seven cipher suites: TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256 ({0xCC, 0xA8}), TLS_ECDHE_ECDSA_WITH_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256 ({0xCC, 0xA9}), TLS_DHE_RSA_WITH_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256 ({0xCC, 0xAA}), TLS_PSK_WITH_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256 ({0xCC, 0xAB}), TLS_ECDHE_PSK_WITH_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256 ({0xCC, 0xAC}), TLS_DHE_PSK_WITH_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256 ({0xCC, 0xAD}) and TLS_RSA_PSK_WITH_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256 ({0xCC, 0xAE}).

The DHE_RSA, ECDHE_RSA, ECDHE_ECDSA, PSK, ECDHE_PSK, DHE_PSK and RSA_PSK key exchanges for these cipher suites are unaltered, so they are performed as defined in RFC 5246, RFC 4492 and RFC 5489. The pseudorandom function for all seven suites is the TLS PRF with SHA-256 as the hash function.
sections.plainLanguage: Seven cipher suites are defined, one for each way of agreeing on keys. The key exchange itself is unchanged from the earlier TLS specifications, and the PRF that expands the key material uses SHA-256.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
ChaCha20 follows the same basic principle as Salsa20, a cipher with significant security review. At the time of writing there were no known significant security problems with either cipher, and ChaCha20 is shown to be more resistant in certain attacks than Salsa20. ChaCha20 was also used as the core of the BLAKE hash function, a SHA-3 finalist that received considerable cryptanalytic attention.

Poly1305 is designed so that forged messages are rejected with a probability of 1-(n/2^107), where n is the maximum length of the input to Poly1305. For TLS and DTLS that gives a maximum forgery probability of about 1 in 2^93.

The cipher suites require that a nonce is never repeated under the same key. The design ensures this by using the TLS sequence number, which is unique and does not wrap.

The RFC also notes the limits of the scheme. An AEAD such as ChaCha20-Poly1305 is not intended to hide the lengths of plaintexts, and the side-channel discussion here is about timing and cache side channels rather than traffic analysis. Traffic analysis is a valid concern but is outside the scope of the AEAD, and the RFC says it is addressed elsewhere in future versions of TLS. Otherwise the document introduces no security considerations beyond those that follow from the AEAD_CHACHA20_POLY1305 construction itself, so the reader is directed to the security considerations of RFC 7539.
sections.plainLanguage: The two algorithms had no known significant weaknesses at the time of writing, and the chance of forging a valid tag is about 1 in 2^93. The one thing an attacker must never see is the same nonce used twice with the same key, and the record number guarantees that. The scheme does not hide how long the messages are.

items.title: Nonce uniqueness
items.text: A nonce must never repeat under the same key, and the TLS sequence number makes it unique.

items.title: Forgery probability
items.text: Poly1305 rejects a forged message with a probability of about 1 in 2^93.

items.title: Side channels
items.text: The concern is timing and cache behaviour, not traffic analysis.

items.title: Plaintext length
items.text: An AEAD does not hide how long the messages are.
